tagline: A short letter to a young church in the Lycus valley, insisting that Christ is supreme over all things and that believers already have everything in him.
overview:
Colossians is a letter written in Paul's name, with Timothy, to a small church in the town of Colossae in Asia Minor (modern Turkey). Paul had never visited it. The church had been planted by Epaphras, one of its own people, who had come to Paul in prison with news of the believers' faith and love and, it seems, with a worry: some teaching was circulating that promised the Colossians a fuller spiritual life through special visions, food rules, holy days, severe treatment of the body, and attention to angels and spiritual powers.

Paul's answer is not first a list of counterarguments but a portrait of Christ. In one of the great passages of the New Testament (1:15-20), Christ is the image of the invisible God, the one through whom and for whom all things were made, the one in whom all things hold together, the head of the church, the firstborn from the dead, and the one through whom God reconciles all things by the blood of his cross. If all the fullness of God dwells in him bodily (2:9), then the believer who belongs to him lacks nothing. The powers have been disarmed at the cross (2:15), and rules about eating and drinking are shadows of a reality that has already arrived.

The second half of the letter shows what that means in ordinary life. Believers have been raised with Christ, so they are to set their minds on things above, put to death the old ways of sexual sin, greed, anger, and lying, and put on compassion, forgiveness, and love (3:1-17). The letter then addresses the household (wives and husbands, children and fathers, slaves and masters), asks for prayer, and closes with a warm list of names that ties it closely to the short letter to Philemon.
author:
The letter names Paul and Timothy as its senders (1:1), and Paul signs the closing greeting in his own hand (4:18). The early church received it as Paul's without dispute, and it was included in the earliest collections of his letters.

Since the nineteenth century many scholars have questioned that. They point to a style that differs from the letters everyone accepts as Paul's (long sentences strung together with relative clauses, and fewer of Paul's usual connecting words), to a picture of Christ as head over the cosmos and the church that goes beyond what those letters say, and to statements that believers have already been raised with Christ (2:12; 3:1), where Romans 6 speaks of resurrection as still to come. On this view a follower of Paul wrote in his name after his death, a practice known in the ancient world. Others answer that style shifts with subject and with the secretary a writer used, that the letter's theology grows out of Paul's own, and above all that the personal details match Philemon, a letter almost all scholars accept, so closely (Onesimus, Archippus, Epaphras, Aristarchus, Mark, Luke, Demas) that a forger would have had to copy them with unusual care. A middle position, argued by James D. G. Dunn among others, suggests Timothy composed the letter during Paul's lifetime with Paul's approval, which would explain both the Pauline substance and the different style.
date: If Paul wrote Colossians, he wrote it from prison (4:3, 10, 18). As with Philippians, the place is debated. The traditional view places him in Rome around AD 60 to 62. Others suggest Ephesus in the mid-50s, much nearer Colossae, which would make the travel of Epaphras and Onesimus easier to explain; a few suggest Caesarea around AD 57 to 59. Scholars who think a follower of Paul wrote the letter usually date it in the decades after his death, often around AD 70 to 90. Tacitus records that Laodicea, Colossae's neighbor, was destroyed by an earthquake around AD 60, and the region seems to have been hit hard; the letter's silence about such a disaster has been used on both sides of the dating question.
setting:
Colossae lay in the Lycus River valley in the region of Phrygia, in the Roman province of Asia, roughly 120 miles (190 km) east of Ephesus. Two larger cities stood a short distance away: Laodicea, about ten miles (16 km) west, and Hierapolis, a little farther to the northwest. Both are named in the letter (2:1; 4:13, 15-16). Centuries earlier Colossae had been an important town on the road through the valley, known for its wool and dyed cloth, but by Paul's day it had been overshadowed by Laodicea. The site near modern Honaz in Turkey has never been fully excavated.

The population was mixed: native Phrygians, Greeks, and a substantial Jewish community, since the Seleucid king Antiochus III had settled Jewish families in Phrygia and Lydia around 200 BC. Local religion included the worship of many gods, interest in spiritual powers and protection from them, and in the wider region a strong tradition of calling on angels. The church itself seems to have been mostly Gentile (1:21, 27; 2:13). It met in homes, including that of Philemon (Philemon 2), and was cared for from a distance by Epaphras, who also labored for the believers in Laodicea and Hierapolis (4:12-13).

What exactly the teaching troubling the church was, often called the Colossian heresy, is one of the most debated questions in New Testament study, because Paul only alludes to it. It involved philosophy and human tradition (2:8), the spiritual forces or elemental principles of the world (2:8, 20), food and drink laws, festivals, new moons, and Sabbaths (2:16), false humility, the worship of angels, and visions (2:18), and harsh treatment of the body (2:21-23). J. B. Lightfoot in the nineteenth century saw a blend of Jewish practice with early Gnostic speculation. Others see a form of Jewish mysticism that sought visionary ascent to join the worship of angels in heaven, reading the phrase about angels that way. Clinton Arnold has argued for a local folk religion that mixed Jewish, pagan, and Christian elements and called on angels for protection. Morna Hooker asked whether there was an organized false teaching at all, suggesting Paul may be warning against general pressures from surrounding Jewish and pagan religion. Each reading explains some features better than others, and Paul's answer is the same on any of them.
purpose: Paul writes to strengthen a church he has never seen, to thank God for its faith, and to guard it from being taken captive by teaching that would add requirements or spiritual experiences to Christ as though he were not enough (2:4, 8). He wants them to know Christ as the one in whom all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge are hidden (2:3), to continue in him as they received him (2:6-7), and to live out their new life in their households and before outsiders. The letter also introduces Tychicus, who carried it, and commends Onesimus, the runaway slave of Philemon, now returning as a faithful brother (4:7-9).
story: Colossians belongs to the later part of Paul's ministry, after the travels in Acts 13 to 20, when the gospel had taken root in the cities of Asia Minor through the work of Paul and his coworkers. It is one of the four Prison Letters, with Ephesians, Philippians, and Philemon, and it is especially close to Ephesians, which shares much of its content and language. In the larger story of the Bible it shows the church, a mixed community of Jews and Gentiles, learning that the Messiah of Israel is also the Lord of creation. The creation of Genesis 1 and the wisdom of Proverbs 8, through which God made the world, stand behind its portrait of Christ, and the shadows of Israel's calendar and food laws are said to point forward to him (2:17).
christ: Colossians contains some of the highest statements about Christ in the New Testament. He is “the image of the invisible God, the firstborn over all creation” (1:15). All things were created through him and for him, and in him all things hold together (1:16-17). “For in Christ all the fullness of the Deity dwells in bodily form” (2:9). He is also the crucified one, who reconciled all things by the blood of his cross, canceled the record of debt against us, and disarmed the powers (1:20; 2:14-15). He is risen and seated at the right hand of God (3:1), he is the believer's life (3:4), and he will appear in glory. The church's confession that Christ is fully God and fully human, creator and redeemer, finds some of its clearest New Testament grounding here.
reading: Read Colossians as a real letter, written with a particular threat in view that its first readers knew better than we do. Because Paul only alludes to the teaching he opposes, be cautious about reconstructing it in detail; read what he says about Christ as the main thing, not as a reply to be decoded. Watch for the letter's key words: fullness and filling, wisdom and knowledge, mystery, the head and the body, and putting off and putting on. The letter moves from who Christ is (chapters 1 and 2) to how believers live (chapters 3 and 4), and the second half depends on the first. A common misreading treats the household instructions in 3:18 to 4:1 as a timeless blueprint detached from their setting, or dismisses them as simply the culture of the day; both skip the question of how Paul's phrase in the Lord reshapes each relationship.

structure.title: Greeting, thanks, and prayer
structure.summary: Paul greets the church, thanks God for their faith, love, and hope, and prays that they will be filled with the knowledge of God's will.

structure.title: The supremacy of Christ
structure.summary: The great hymn to Christ as creator and reconciler, followed by its meaning for the Colossians, who have been reconciled if they continue in the faith.

structure.title: Paul's labor for the church
structure.summary: Paul describes his sufferings and his commission to make known the mystery, Christ in you, and his struggle for churches he has never seen.

structure.title: Complete in Christ
structure.summary: Believers are to continue in Christ, in whom the fullness of God dwells, and refuse teaching that binds them to food laws, holy days, visions, and human regulations.

structure.title: The new life
structure.summary: Raised with Christ, believers put off the old self and put on the new, live in love and thankfulness, order their households in the Lord, and pray and speak wisely.

structure.title: Messengers and greetings
structure.summary: Paul commends Tychicus and Onesimus, sends greetings from his coworkers, and closes with a greeting in his own hand.

themes.title: The supremacy of Christ
themes.body: The letter's center is Christ's preeminence over everything: creation, the powers, the church, and death. Nothing in heaven or on earth stands outside his authority, and nothing can be added to him. Every warning in the letter flows from this conviction, and so does its confidence.

themes.title: Fullness
themes.body: Words for fullness and filling run through the letter. God was pleased to have all his fullness dwell in Christ (1:19; 2:9), and believers have been made complete in him (2:10). Paul prays that they will be filled with the knowledge of God's will (1:9). The false teaching promised a fuller spiritual life; Paul answers that they already have fullness in Christ and need only to grow into it.

themes.title: Victory over the powers
themes.body: The ancient world felt surrounded by spiritual forces, rulers, and authorities. Colossians says that these were created through and for Christ (1:16) and that at the cross he disarmed them and made a public spectacle of them (2:15). Believers who have died with Christ are no longer subject to them or to regulations based on them (2:20).

themes.title: Dying and rising with Christ
themes.body: Paul describes conversion and baptism as being buried and raised with Christ (2:12). The new life that results is hidden with Christ in God and will be revealed when he appears (3:3-4). The ethical instructions of chapter 3 rest on this: put to death what belongs to the old life, because you have already died, and put on the new self, because you have already been raised.

themes.title: The new humanity
themes.body: In the renewed self, there is no Greek or Jew, circumcised or uncircumcised, barbarian, Scythian, slave, or free, but Christ is all and in all (3:11). The church is a single body under one head, marked by compassion, forgiveness, peace, and thankful worship. The household instructions that follow apply this new identity to the most ordinary relationships.

keyChapters.why: The hymn to Christ as the image of God, creator, head of the church, and reconciler of all things (1:15-20), with Paul's prayer and his account of his ministry.
Paul's answer to the false teaching: all the fullness of God dwells in Christ, the powers were disarmed at the cross, and the rules are shadows of the reality.
The new life of those raised with Christ, marked by putting off the old self and putting on love, peace, and thankfulness, with instructions for the household.
